name: Spack
description: Spack is a multi-platform package manager that builds and installs multiple versions and configurations of software. It works on Linux, macOS, Windows, and many supercomputers.
description_good_justification: The README describes what Spack does: a package manager that builds and installs multiple versions and configurations of software.
interact_justification: The README points to the documentation, GitHub Discussions, Slack, and Matrix for questions and feedback, and to GitHub issues and pull requests for bug reports and contributions.
contribution_justification: The Contribution Guide is part of Spack's documentation and is linked from the README and .github/CONTRIBUTING.md.
floss_license_justification: Spack is dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 and MIT, at the user's option (see COPYRIGHT, LICENSE-APACHE, LICENSE-MIT).
floss_license_osi_justification: Both Apache-2.0 and MIT are approved by the Open Source Initiative.
license_location_justification: LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT are at the top level of the repository.
repo_public_justification: The repository is public on GitHub: https://github.com/spack/spack
repo_track_justification: Git on GitHub tracks every change, with author and date.
repo_interim_justification: The develop branch is public, so interim work between releases is visible to everyone.
version_tags_justification: Releases are identified by git tags such as v1.2.0, v1.2.1 and v1.2.2.
release_notes_justification: Each release has human-written notes on its GitHub release page (for example v1.2.0, v1.2.1 and v1.2.2) that summarize the major changes and bug fixes. They are not raw git log output. CHANGELOG.md also collects the notes for most releases.
report_tracker_justification: Bug reports are filed as GitHub issues, using the templates in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE: https://github.com/spack/spack/issues
vulnerability_report_process_justificati: SECURITY.md describes how to report a vulnerability.
vulnerability_report_private_justificati: SECURITY.md directs reporters to GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.
test_justification: Spack has a pytest-based automated test suite, run with `spack unit-test` (lib/spack/spack/test).
test_invocation_justification: The test suite is run with `spack unit-test`, which wraps pytest, or with pytest directly.
test_continuous_integration_justificatio: GitHub Actions runs the unit tests on Linux, macOS and Windows for every pull request (.github/workflows/unit_tests.yaml).
static_analysis_justification: Ruff (lint rules) and mypy (type checking) run through `spack style`, plus pylint, in CI (.github/workflows/prechecks.yml) on every pull request and on pushes to develop and releases/** (ci.yaml), so release branches are analyzed before a release.
contribution_requirements_justification: The Contribution Guide is explicit about how contributions must be written. Its Style Tests section requires PEP 8 conformance, enforced with Ruff, and mypy type checking for changes to the Spack library, and shows how to check and fix style with `spack style`.
documentation_basics_justification: The documentation at https://spack.readthedocs.io (source in lib/spack/docs) covers installing Spack and its prerequisites (getting_started, installing_prerequisites), basic usage (spec_syntax, installing, environments_basics), configuration, and a FAQ and help page (frequently_asked_questions, getting_help).
documentation_interface_justification: The documentation includes a command reference generated from the code (command_index.rst, built from `spack commands` in lib/spack/docs/conf.py), reference pages for the configuration files (config_yaml, packages_yaml, toolchains_yaml, include_yaml, env_vars_yaml) and for the spec syntax (spec_syntax), and API documentation generated with sphinx-apidoc.
sites_https_justification: The project website (https://spack.io), the repository (https://github.com/spack/spack), the documentation (https://spack.readthedocs.io) and the release downloads (https://github.com/spack/spack/releases) are all served over HTTPS.
discussion_justification: Discussion happens on GitHub issues, pull requests and GitHub Discussions. These are searchable, every thread has its own URL, anyone with a GitHub account can take part, and no proprietary client software is needed.
english_justification: The documentation, README, contribution guide and issue templates are written in English, and bug reports and discussions on GitHub are in English.
maintained_justification: Spack is actively developed: there were 221 commits to develop in the last 90 days from many contributors, and releases v1.2.0 (2026-06-22), v1.2.1 (2026-07-06) and v1.2.2 (2026-07-20) came out this summer.
version_unique_justification: Each release has a unique version identifier and a matching git tag, for example v1.2.0, v1.2.1 and v1.2.2, and release branches such as releases/v1.2.
version_semver_justification: Releases use the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering of SemVer, for example 1.2.2. Minor releases (1.x.0) add features and patch releases (1.x.y) carry fixes, including security updates.
report_process_justification: Users submit bug reports as GitHub issues, using the bug report and feature request templates in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Package build and test errors are reported in the spack/spack-packages repository, which the issue chooser links to.
report_responses_justification: Of the 170 issues labeled bug that were opened between 2025-10-16 and 2026-08-16 (2 to 12 months ago), 126 (74%) have at least one comment. Of the other 44, 19 were closed without a comment and 25 are still open.
enhancement_responses_justification: Of the 48 issues labeled feature (the label the feature request template applies) that were opened between 2025-10-16 and 2026-08-16 (2 to 12 months ago), 32 (67%) have at least one comment.
report_archive_justification: Bug reports and comments are GitHub issues, which are public, searchable, and each have their own URL, so they form a permanent public archive.
build_justification: Spack is written in Python and runs directly from a git checkout.
build_common_tools_justification: Spack needs no build to use. For the optional wheel, pyproject.toml uses Hatchling, a standard build backend.
build_floss_tools_justification: Spack needs no build to use. The optional wheel build uses Hatchling, which is FLOSS.
test_most_justification: Coverage is measured in CI with branch coverage enabled (pyproject.toml) and reported to Codecov (https://app.codecov.io/gh/spack/spack). Codecov reported about 85% overall coverage when checked on 2026-10-16.
test_policy_justification: The Contribution Guide's Unit Tests section says: if you are modifying core Spack libraries or adding new functionality, please add new unit tests for your feature and consider strengthening existing tests. Contributions are expected to pass the CI test suite.
tests_are_added_justification: In the 6 months before 2026-10-16, 396 non-merge commits on develop changed Spack library source; 266 of them (67%) also changed files under lib/spack/spack/test.
tests_documented_added_justification: The Contribution Guide, which .github/CONTRIBUTING.md points contributors to, states the policy in its Unit Tests section: add new unit tests when modifying core libraries or adding functionality, and it explains how to run and write them.
warnings_justification: Spack uses linters and a type checker: Ruff (lint rules E, F, W and I, configured in pyproject.toml) and mypy, both run through `spack style`. CI also runs vermin (Python version compatibility) and slotscheck (.github/workflows/prechecks.yml).
warnings_fixed_justification: The `style` job in .github/workflows/prechecks.yml runs `spack style` on every pull request, and the Contribution Guide says a PR must comply with PEP 8 and, if it changes the Spack library, type-check with mypy in order to be accepted.
warnings_strict_justification: Beyond Ruff's default rules, the project enables the isort import-order rules, runs mypy with errors enabled for the spack and spack_repo modules, checks Python-version compatibility with vermin and __slots__ use with slotscheck.
crypto_published_justification: Spack uses only published, expert-reviewed algorithms and protocols. Checksums use the SHA-2 family from Python's hashlib (package versions are checksummed with sha256; md5 is accepted for legacy packages but flagged as deprecated with a warning). Spec hashes use SHA-1 for identification, not for authentication. HTTPS uses TLS through Python's ssl module with certificate verification on by default (config:verify_ssl: true), and binary cache signing and verification use OpenPGP through GnuPG.
crypto_call_justification: Spack's own code does not implement cryptographic primitives. It calls Python's hashlib, ssl and secrets modules and the curl and GnuPG programs. See lib/spack/spack/util/crypto.py, which wraps hashlib, and lib/spack/spack/util/web.py, which builds on ssl.create_default_context.
crypto_floss_justification: All of Spack's cryptographic functionality can be provided by FLOSS. It uses Python's hashlib and ssl modules (backed by OpenSSL), curl for downloads, and GnuPG for signing and verifying binary caches. Spack can build and bootstrap GnuPG itself (lib/spack/spack/bootstrap/core.py).
crypto_keylength_justification: Spack generates its own keys in one place, `spack gpg create`, which creates RSA keys with a fixed Key-Length of 4096 (lib/spack/spack/util/gpg.py), above the NIST minimum through 2030. Neither that command nor Spack's configuration offers any way to choose a smaller key length, so smaller key lengths are not available through Spack. TLS uses Python's ssl.create_default_context() with no key-size or cipher overrides, so Spack inherits the defaults of Python and OpenSSL.
crypto_working_justification: Spack's default security mechanisms are sha256 checksums for downloads and bootstrap binaries, TLS with certificate verification, and OpenPGP signatures through GnuPG. None depends on a broken algorithm. MD5 is accepted only for legacy package checksums, where Spack prints a deprecation warning when it is used and the audit in lib/spack/spack/audit.py flags packages that use it. Elsewhere MD5 is used only for non-security purposes: a short identifier for a bootstrap environment path (bootstrap/environment.py), a directory hash used by tests (util/filesystem.py), and the file checksum computed by the CDash reporter (reporters/cdash.py).
crypto_weaknesses_justification: Spack's default security mechanisms use sha256 for download and binary cache integrity, TLS with certificate verification, and OpenPGP signatures through GnuPG. The only SHA-1 use is in spack.util.hash.b32_hash, which produces the base32 spec hashes and other identifiers (spec.py, environment.py, package_hash.py, config.py, repo.py, solver/asp.py), and in short names for stage directories. These label and look up things; they are not signatures, authentication or integrity checks, so they are not security mechanisms.
crypto_pfs_justification: Spack does not implement any key agreement protocol. Its only network encryption is TLS, handled by Python's ssl module and OpenSSL through ssl.create_default_context() in lib/spack/spack/util/web.py, and by curl. Spack sets no cipher, protocol-version or key-exchange options of its own, so key agreement is left to those libraries' defaults.
crypto_password_storage_justification: Spack has no user accounts and does not authenticate external users, so it stores no user passwords. It only sends credentials of its own user to services the user configures, such as OCI and S3 mirrors. For those it reads the password or token from an environment variable named on the command line (--oci-password-variable, --s3-access-token-variable) and does not store a password hash.
crypto_random_justification: Spack does not generate cryptographic keys or nonces itself. Keys are generated by GnuPG (`spack gpg create`). Where Spack needs unpredictable values it uses the secrets module and uuid.uuid4, which draw from the operating system's secure random source (for temporary file names in fetch_strategy.py and util/filesystem.py, and for identifiers). The insecure random module is used only for non-security purposes: shuffling the solver problem (solver/asp.py) and retry-delay jitter (util/web.py).
delivery_mitm_justification: The default mirror (https://mirror.spack.io, etc/spack/defaults/base/mirrors.yaml) and the bootstrap sources (share/spack/bootstrap/*/metadata.yaml) also use https URLs, and TLS certificate verification is on by default (config:verify_ssl: true).
delivery_unsigned_justification: Spack does not fetch hashes over plain http and use them unchecked. The sha256 sums for the bootstrap binaries (clingo, GnuPG, patchelf) are stored in the Spack repository itself (share/spack/bootstrap/*/*.json) and are delivered with the source over HTTPS. Package checksums are stored in the package recipes, and binary caches can be verified with GnuPG signatures.
no_leaked_credentials_justification: A search of develop (2026-10-16) for private keys and API tokens found none.
static_analysis_common_vulnerabilities_j: Not yet, we plan to implement in the future.
static_analysis_fixed_justification: The static analysis tools in use (Ruff, mypy, pylint) check style, types and basic code errors, not vulnerabilities, so they do not report exploitable vulnerabilities. Any finding fails the style check in CI and must be fixed before a pull request is merged.
static_analysis_often_justification: The style job in .github/workflows/prechecks.yml runs on every pull request and on every push to develop and releases/** (ci.yaml). On pull requests it checks the files changed in the commit.
dynamic_analysis_justification: The automated test suite (pytest, lib/spack/spack/test) runs in CI on every pull request and on pushes to develop and releases/**. Codecov reports about 85% coverage (checked 2026-10-16) with branch measurement enabled in pyproject.toml.
dynamic_analysis_unsafe_justification: Spack is written in Python. The repository has no first-party C, C++, Rust or Go source.
dynamic_analysis_enable_assertions_justi: The library contains about 220 assert statements outside the tests. Python runs them unless started with -O, and the test suite in CI is run without it, so they are active during testing.
dynamic_analysis_fixed_justification: No fuzzer or other tool that varies inputs to look for vulnerabilities is used. The test suite finds functional bugs, and a failing test blocks a pull request until it is fixed.
